question: What does sabq literally and figuratively mean?

positions.position: Sabq literally means going or reaching ahead in travel or a race, then extends to precedence in rank, good, and reward.
positions.reasons: Al-Bursevī says the travel sense is primary; al-Rāghib calls attaining excellence a borrowing. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites al-Nābigha's image of a swift horse reaching the hunt before the others to explain rank precedence. The Study Quran gives go first, outstrip, and win a race. Al-Iṣlāḥī rejects reading the class names as spatial positions before God.

question: Who are the forerunners, and in what do they precede others?

positions.position: They are the first to believe in God and respond to the prophets, among every community or the earliest Muslims.
positions.reasons: Qatāda and Ibn ʿAbbās say every nation contributes forerunners; al-Wāḥidī cites 9:100 for Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation. Muqātil and ʿIkrima stress immediate response when truth appears; al-Māwardī specifies Islam before Muhammad's emigration or arrival, before hope or fear could move converts. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the class continues into Muhammad's community. Al-Iṣlāḥī stresses early supporters' costly service with person and wealth and cites 57:10: pre-conquest spending and fighting ranked higher, though both groups receive good reward. Al-Sulamī differentiates prophets first in faith in God from truthful persons and martyrs first in faith in prophets. Ibn Zayd's knowledge prevailing over desire marks two Paradise groups, with desire's victory placing a person in Hell.

positions.position: They hasten to every good deed and all that God commands.
positions.reasons: Al-Quraẓī and Ibn Kaysān make the scope comprehensive; Jishumī and Ṭabrisī prefer it because it includes the narrower examples. Ibn Kathīr says reward matches deeds, citing 3:133 and 57:22; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 35:32, 2:148, 23:61, and 57:21. Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Baghawī cite 23:61. Al-Kashshāf stresses sincere, energetic response; Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes avoiding sins; Ibn ʿĀshūr says omitting the object generalizes every virtuous competition, as in 83:26. Al-Tustarī's and other specified examples can be read within this broad class, according to al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī.

positions.position: They are first to Paradise and God's mercy because they first believed or obeyed in this life.
positions.reasons: Al-Kalbī and al-Rabīʿ explicitly pair worldly response with Paradise. Al-Zajjāj, al-Jishumī, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī pair obedience and good deeds with mercy and forgiveness. Al-Qummī applies Paradise to the second occurrence; al-Ṭabrisī says their model conduct earns the highest rank. Al-Dāmghānī and al-Bayḍāwī give Paradise as the goal.

positions.position: They hasten to mosques and to go out in God's cause.
positions.reasons: ʿUthmān ibn Abī Sawda gives both actions; al-Wāḥidī describes the first ranks of worshippers and fighters. A report raised through Ibn ʿAbbās has the forerunner enter the mosque first and leave last; al-Ālūsī gives no grading. Mujāhid combines first jihad with early prayer departure.

positions.position: They are the earliest Companions who prayed toward both qiblas.
positions.reasons: Ibn Sīrīn's identification signals the Companions' early adherence; al-Wāḥidī connects it to Ibn ʿAbbās's early-belief view. Al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Ālūsī connect it with 9:100; the latter names early Emigrants and Helpers.

positions.position: They are those who were first to emigrate.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās says worldly precedence in migration yields precedence in the afterlife; Ibn ʿĀshūr includes the first Emigrants and Helpers and cites 9:100.

positions.position: They take precedence in the five daily prayers.
positions.reasons: Attributed repeatedly to ʿAlī; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī treats it as an illustrative instance of the general meaning.

positions.position: They are first to repent and perform righteous works.
positions.reasons: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr cites the commands to race toward forgiveness in 3:133 and 57:21; al-Qurṭubī also cites 23:61. Al-Qushayrī adds regret for sin.

positions.position: They are the prophets, leaders of their religious communities.
positions.reasons: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb gives this identification. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī explain that prophets lead adherents of their religions. The Study Quran says many commentators include prophets; other views include saints, truthful persons and martyrs, while some put prophets beyond the forerunners.

positions.position: They are first to undertake jihad.
positions.reasons: Attributed to al-Ḍaḥḥāk in several sources; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows that this may be an instance of the general sense.

positions.position: They are the people of the Qurʾān.
positions.reasons: Kaʿb says they will be crowned on Resurrection Day; al-Baghawī specifies reciters.

positions.position: They accept what is due, give when asked, and judge others as themselves.
positions.reasons: A prophetic report is cited by al-Mahdawī and others; Ibn Kathīr's ʿĀʾisha version says they reach the Resurrection shade first. Wording varies between accepting a due right and accepting truth.

positions.position: They were first to acquire virtue, firm knowledge, and piety; their precedence is in rank.
positions.reasons: Al-Bayḍāwī speaks of virtues and perfections. Al-Bursevī distinguishes rank from chronological priority; al-Ālūsī specifies certain knowledge and degrees of piety beyond faith. The Study Quran reports a virtue reading. Al-Qushayrī also reports people promised the highest reward who hasten to their allotted good.

positions.position: They were early and persistent doers of good throughout life.
positions.reasons: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shumayṭ and Shumayṭ ibn ʿAjlān contrast this group with late repenters on the right and lifelong evildoers on the left; the accounts differ slightly in the named transmitter and description of youth.

positions.position: They are the higher people of Paradise, including prophets, the truthful, and martyrs.
positions.reasons: Ibn Kathīr calls them a smaller elite nearer God, after the right and left classes. Al-Suddī calls them people of ʿIlliyyīn; the Study Quran connects their upper heavenly residence with 83:18. Kuran Yolu says they are the leading portion of those receiving records in the right hand, citing 56:11 and 56:88; al-Sāmarrāʾī calls them creation's highest.

positions.position: They are spiritual knowers and devoted servants brought near by divine favor.
positions.reasons: Al-Tustarī and al-Sulamī say God chose them for friendship or guardianship before their existence. Al-Jurayrī says they have no concern besides God; Abū ʿAlī al-Jawzajānī names true knowledge, sincere worship, longing and love. Al-Qushayrī includes sincerity and high aspiration; the Study Quran names an elite understanding religion's inner meaning.

positions.position: Joshua, the believer of Yā Sīn, and ʿAlī were the first for Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad respectively.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās names Joshua son of Nun, the believer of Yā Sīn, and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib; the reports say each preceded his community.

positions.position: Ḥizqīl, Ḥabīb al-Najjār, and ʿAlī are named as those who preceded their communities.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās's reported list includes Pharaoh's believer, the Yā Sīn companion, and ʿAlī; al-Ālūsī adds that ʿAlī is best of them and cites 36:20. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this as a revelation identification.

positions.position: Ḥizqīl, Ḥabīb al-Najjār, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar are singled out.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās's report places Ḥizqīl with Moses' or Pharaoh's people and Ḥabīb with Jesus' people, then Abū Bakr and ʿUmar with Muhammad's people.

positions.position: Adam's slain son, Pharaoh's believer, Ḥabīb al-Najjār, and ʿAlī are four forerunners.
positions.reasons: Abū Jaʿfar identifies one pioneer in each named setting; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says al-Ṣādiq also transmits this account.

positions.position: They are monotheists who pass beyond both worlds through annihilation in God.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī says they outstrip both other groups.

positions.position: Abū Bakr and ʿAlī are among the foremost in belief and Paradise.
positions.reasons: Muqātil singles out these two as first in belief in God and His Messenger among their communities.

positions.position: ʿAlī and his Shiʿa precede to Paradise and are brought near.
positions.reasons: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās attributes this identification to Gabriel speaking to the Prophet; another report from ʿAlī says the verse was revealed about him.

positions.position: The Prophet, Salmān, Bilāl, and Ṣuhayb are the foremost of Arabs, Persians, Abyssinians, and Romans.
positions.reasons: Reported as a prophetic saying, assigning one named forerunner to each people.

positions.position: Abū Jaʿfar identifies his own community as the foremost and the last.
positions.reasons: Abū Jaʿfar says, 'We are the foremost, and we are the last ones.'

positions.position: They bypass the Reckoning and enter Paradise directly.
positions.reasons: The Study Quran reports this view, distinguishing them from right- and left-hand groups who stand for judgment.

turns_on: The notes distinguish comprehensive good deeds from particular acts, early faith across communities from early Muslims, precedence in time from rank, and differing named pioneers; some treat narrower identifications as examples.

question: How does the repetition of al-sābiqūn work?

positions.position: The first al-sābiqūn is the subject and the second its predicate, acclaiming a renowned rank beyond fuller description.
positions.reasons: Sībawayh's analysis is preferred by Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī prefer this over emphasis. Al-Kashshāf, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Samīn, and others compare Abū al-Najm's 'my poetry is my poetry' to repeated renown. Al-Rāzī says their state surpasses knowledge; al-Qāshānī says no praise can encompass it. Al-Iṣlāḥī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say no predicate better conveys their rank. Al-Ālūsī says no different objects need be supplied. Ibn ʿĀshūr's general comments, citing al-Sakkākī, connect rhetorical analysis with Qur'anic inimitability.

positions.position: The second noun emphatically repeats the first; 'those are the brought-near' supplies the predicate.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, al-Ṭabarī and others give this parse. Al-Kashshāf places a sound pause after the second noun and says it parallels the other groups. Al-Samīn describes the next words as a new clause in predicate position and compares 7:26. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the repetition expresses amazement. Al-Ālūsī rejects it for weakening the division and later contrast; al-Nasafī favors the predicate parse.

positions.position: The second al-sābiqūn predicates a different precedence: first in faith or obedience here, then first in mercy or Paradise.
positions.reasons: Al-Zajjāj and his transmitters distinguish obedience and mercy; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn allow faith, obedience, or good works paired with Paradise or mercy. Ṣāḥib al-Murshid gives obedience/mercy and good/Paradise. Al-Ālūsī prefers the complete predicate without supplying different objects.

positions.position: The second noun is an adjective modifying the first, with the predicate following.
positions.reasons: Some grammarians give this parse. Abū Isḥāq allows it; Abū Ḥayyān allows it when the two words have different objects. Al-Ālūsī defends adjectival analysis by saying the definite article need not be relative here. Al-Samīn rejects a bare adjective as pointless and suggests its proponents meant emphasis.

positions.position: The first noun is coordinated with the right-hand group, or stands as a separate clause after a pause.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī reports coordination with the preceding right-hand people before the clause 'those are the brought-near.' Al-Samīn rejects the pause-and-new-clause version because it strains coordination and requires an insertion.

positions.position: Each group label serves as predicate of an omitted topic; the repeated label introduces its description.
positions.reasons: Al-Irshād says the division naturally names categories before describing them; earlier descriptions preview the other groups' eventual states, while the forerunners receive description immediately. Al-Ālūsī favors this sequence. A criticism says the parse only identifies groups and leaves the two earlier questions unexplained; another analysis allows the questions to modify prior labels after an implied saying.

positions.position: The phrase tacitly follows an omitted question, 'What are the forerunners?'
positions.reasons: Al-Bursevī infers that question from the two preceding 'what are the companions of the right/left?' questions.

turns_on: The disputed syntax is subject and predicate, emphatic repetition with a following predicate, adjective plus predicate, or an ellipsis; the subject-predicate parse may praise renowned rank or assign different objects to each occurrence.

question: What is their rank among the three groups?

positions.position: They are the third, most excellent class, brought near above the companions of the right.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī calls them the third group in 56:7; Ibn Kathīr makes them a smaller elite including messengers, prophets, truthful people and martyrs. Al-Biqāʿī links them to the first two gardens in al-Raḥmān and calls them people of the heart. Kuran Yolu makes them the leading part of those given the right-hand record, citing 56:11 and 56:88. Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts their highest Paradise rank with the lesser rank of the right-hand group. The Study Quran reports the highest parts of Heaven.

question: How can the forerunners describe the soul's inner faculties?

positions.position: The spirit races through care, the heart through guarding, and the limbs through service.
positions.reasons: Al-Jurayrī pairs these with modesty, purity, and recompense as their respective gifts.

question: What brings the forerunners near to God?

positions.position: Precedence in obedience and good deeds is answered by precedence in mercy, honor, and Paradise.
positions.reasons: Al-Kalbī and al-Rabīʿ align worldly and afterlife precedence. Ibn Kathīr says recompense matches deeds, citing 3:133 and 57:22; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī pairs works with corresponding forgiveness and mercy, citing 57:21.

positions.position: God's choice and gift bring them near; their attributed racing does not itself produce nearness.
positions.reasons: Al-Sulamī says divine friendship was given before their existence. Al-Qāsim reasons that, though God attributes racing to servants, their act itself cannot make them near or it would truly belong to them. Al-Qushayrī reports a promised highest reward and haste toward allotted good.

turns_on: Whether the notes ground nearness in prior divine gift or in recompense corresponding to the servants' deeds.

question: What is reported about the relative numbers of forerunners?

positions.position: Earlier nations have more forerunners, while right-hand people from earlier nations and this community are equal in number.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī reports this from the Prophet and connects the count of right-hand people with 56:39.

question: What is said about a forerunner's light in Paradise?

positions.position: A resident's light identifies him to those below when he leaves his Paradise dwelling.
positions.reasons: A Kufan informant gives this description of a foremost, brought-near resident.

question: How did speakers use the idea of racing to encourage people?

positions.position: They urged others to advance, while one speaker said the brought-near people win the race.
positions.reasons: ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr repeated 'Go ahead, go ahead'; ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Qays answered a question about a race's winner by naming those brought near to God.

question: Why are the forerunners placed after the other groups and described next?

positions.position: The best group is mentioned third so its excellent state can be described next and its merit draw attention.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī says their merit warrants priority before detailing the left; al-Biqāʿī says the highest rank among the right encourages excellence while leaving the left undivided as warning. Al-Bursevī and al-Ālūsī say third placement leads directly into their excellent states. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds curiosity, emulation, and a deliberate unfolding of the three groups through proximity and relative priority.

positions.position: Their known greatness makes an interrogative challenge unnecessary.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī contrasts the question about the right-hand companions in 56:8: people already admit they cannot grasp the forerunners' state. Ibn ʿĀshūr says repeating their name conveys honor more strongly than the exclamatory wording for the right.

turns_on: The notes explain either the delayed placement and immediate description by merit and exhortation, or the absence of an interrogative by their inexpressible rank.

question: What kind of standing do the three groups represent?

positions.position: The classes express moral standing by faith and deeds at Judgment, rather than physical placement before God.
positions.reasons: Al-Iṣlāḥī says Judgment overturns worldly standards, divides humanity in verses 1–10, and raises or abases by faith and deeds; spatial right, left, front, and back make no sense before God. Ibn Zayd distinguishes knowledge ruling desire from desire ruling knowledge; the latter leads to Hell. Al-Itqān says the examples of neglecting obligations, fulfilling them, and exceeding in good deeds illustrate rather than exhaust the classes.

question: How does this threefold grouping connect with other Qurʾānic passages and the sūra?

positions.position: The three groups correspond to the wrongdoers, moderate believers, and those foremost in good in another Qurʾānic division.
positions.reasons: Ibn Kathīr associates the sūra's beginning and end with 35:32, on one reading of 'wronging oneself.' Al-Burhān and al-Itqān make the three classifications exhaustive; al-Itqān says concrete examples do not exhaust the general classes.

positions.position: The three ranks continue al-Raḥmān's gradation of punishment and two levels of gardens.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān calls the sūra Meccan and following al-Raḥmān; he maps unbelievers, lesser believers, and superior believers to its garden pairs and to this sūra's opening and closing groups, citing 55:62. Al-Biqāʿī assigns the forerunners the first two gardens. The Study Quran says al-Wāqiʿa completes al-Raḥmān's Paradise/Hell contrast.

positions.position: The sūra's movement toward judgment organizes the fate of all three classes.
positions.reasons: Al-Iṣlāḥī says verses 1–10 establish Judgment and its threefold evaluation; verse 3's raising and lowering becomes the three groups. The Study Quran identifies their afterlife fates as the sūra's central theme.

positions.position: The few forerunners here occupy a higher degree than other servants mentioned in al-Ṣāffāt.
positions.reasons: Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares the lower degree of servants in 37:40 with the forerunners' highest ranks in Paradise.

turns_on: The notes draw different correspondences: 35:32's moral classes, al-Raḥmān's garden levels, al-Ṣāffāt's ranking, and the sūra's judgment theme.

question: How are people paired within the three classes?

positions.position: Each person is joined with peers who did like deeds.
positions.reasons: Al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr reports the Prophet's explanation of the three classes; Ibn Kathīr connects it to souls paired in 81:7.

question: What report compares righteous humans with angels?

positions.position: God refuses angels' request for the Hereafter in place of Adam's children's worldly goods and does not equate them with righteous offspring of one created by His hand.
positions.reasons: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr recounts three appeals and God's contrast with one created by 'Be,' then recites these verses. Al-Dārimī's version specifies righteous offspring and appears in Refutation of the Jahmiyya.
